meta.title: Economic development, manufacturing and defense, 18 days of posts
meta.subject: economic development policy in Texas — the JETI incentive program and the end of Chapter 313, the Texas Semiconductor Innovation Fund and the Space Commission, manufacturing and the effect of tariffs, defense and aerospace industry and military installations, corporate relocations, and the Governor's economic development office
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 18, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas economic development, manufacturing and defense, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Tariffs are bringing jobs back
lanes.description: Tariffs and Trump's trade policy are reviving American manufacturing, with Texas plants like Peterbilt in Denton adding jobs as proof that the 'gone for good' jobs are returning.

lanes.label: Texas wins investment and relocations
lanes.description: Texas is winning billions in new investment, corporate relocations and factories because of a pro-business climate and Republican leadership, which voters should reward at the ballot box.

lanes.label: Defense and chips industrial buildout
lanes.description: Defense, aerospace, semiconductor and space companies, along with military bases, are the growth engine of Texas and the US, backed by large contracts, venture money and state or federal funds.

lanes.label: Incentives as cronyism and corruption
lanes.description: Government money, whether defense awards, subsidies or federal funding, is flowing to politically connected firms and institutions, which is corruption or taxpayer-funded welfare that needs oversight.

lanes.label: Tariffs and war raise costs
lanes.description: Tariffs, the Iran war, inflation and Fed rate policy are raising prices and straining manufacturers and households, so the claimed jobs gains are oversold.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: NancyH
posts.text:
This is the Peterbilt plant in my hometown of Denton, Texas.
Most people drive past that red oval and never think about what it actually does. This factory is Denton’s largest private employer. Parent company PACCAR has said it added more than 1,000 jobs here and more than 2,000 nationwide after last year’s tariffs on imported medium- and heavy-duty trucks. Peterbilt and Kenworth together move about 30 percent of the freight on American highways. That is not a slogan. That is how groceries, lumber, and medicine get to the rest of the country. 

President Trump is scheduled to tour this plant Thursday and speak to the people who build those trucks. I still cannot quite believe the President of the United States is coming to my town. I hope I can get close enough to see the motorcade. Either way, I will be there to welcome him.

I grew up around this kind of work. You can talk about manufacturing from a podium. It looks different when you live next to the building where the trucks actually roll out.

If you live here, be kind to the workers and the folks running security. This is their workplace first.
#DentonTX #Peterbilt #MadeInAmerica #TexasManufacturing #PresidentTrump

posts.name: Flopping Aces
posts.text:
Military. Energy. Markets. War. The fucking chessboard is moving so fast Washington’s limp-dick process can’t even register one piece before the next one gets slammed across the table.

At the Pentagon, Pete Hegseth dropped a 20% cut in general-and-admiral billets, a new four-star Autonomous Warfare Command, Project Meridian, energy-independent military installations, and plans for the first new domestic military base in roughly four decades. That is a freaking avalanche of military restructuring dumped in one shot. 

Before that shit could even settle, energy got torched. Trump announced a South Korean investment framework hitting roughly $200 billion in U.S. energy projects, including a $22.3 billion Texas power complex and plans involving eight nuclear reactors ... though Seoul says portions remain under review. America’s power map is getting redrawn on a scale that should scare the hell out of every fossilized bureaucrat still clutching their briefing binder. 

Then Treasury shoved another piece: automatic Trump Accounts for more than 60 million additional American children. Tens of millions of kids get yanked into the market through accounts created automatically, with families still required to claim certain benefits such as the federal seed contribution. 

And while all that was detonating, the last U.S. forces got the hell out of Iraq after 23 years. Another giant piece ripped off the board.

That cumulative pattern is the whole story.

Military command. Autonomous warfare. Domestic power generation. Nuclear expansion. Tens of millions of investment accounts. A two-decade deployment ending.

Bang. Bang. Bang. Bang.

The sheer velocity is fucking brutal. Washington is still screaming about yesterday’s move while the hand is already reaching across the board again.

Everyone else is still arguing over the pawn Trump moved yesterday.

He’s already moving the rook.

posts.name: James E. Thorne
posts.text:
Logan’s Inflation Error: Burning Down the House to Roast the Pig

Dallas Fed President ignores its own Trimmed Mean PCE measure at 1.92% in her speech. Ignore the Data, ignore the theory, Demand Rate hikes. This is the Fed. 

Lorie Logan’s speech is a clear example of a senior Fed official unable, or unwilling, to distinguish between higher output generated by investment and expanding supply and higher output driven by excess consumption. That distinction is the entire issue. New factory capacity, inventories, logistics networks, energy infrastructure, and domestic production add to supply and relieve inflation over time. Consumption that persistently outruns available output can create excess demand and sustained price pressure. They are not the same thing.

Yet Logan treats stronger activity as evidence that monetary policy is insufficiently restrictive. Her claim rests in part on the observation that “The Texas Manufacturing Outlook Survey found output accelerated sharply in September.” That is the reveal. An increase in supply is not inflationary. More manufacturing output means more goods, greater capacity, fuller inventories, and fewer shortages, the very process through which an economy relieves price pressure. Logan instead treats stronger production as evidence that demand is overheating.

Her assertion that “without any policy restriction, inflation will likely continue its above-target trend” simply assumes the point at issue. Inflation can remain above target while tariffs, higher energy costs, and other negative supply shocks pass through the economy. That does not establish excess demand. Nor does it demonstrate that rate hikes will improve the real adjustment.

This is classic Keynesian demand-management dogma, observe healthy output and spending, presume excessive demand, and prescribe tighter money. But rate hikes cannot create energy, undo a tariff, rebuild a supply chain, or expand productive capacity. They cannot speed the adjustment to a tariff shock or a negative energy shock.

They can only suppress demand, and, worse, raise the cost of the capital investment, inventories, logistics, factories, and energy infrastructure needed to adapt to those shocks. Higher rates risk delaying the supply response while weakening the economy that is generating it.

Logan wants to burn down the house to roast the pig, use broad demand destruction to attack inflation that may largely reflect supply-side disruptions already working their way through the system. Growth alongside easing inflation is not proof of overheating. It may be evidence that supply is recovering. Her error is to see that recovery, call it inflationary, and then threaten to choke it off.

Opening remarks for moderated conversation at Voices of the Eleventh District https://t.co/EA2j8J8dIx via @DallasFed

posts.name: Owen Gregorian
posts.text:
How a Gen Zer built a $3.7 billion defense tech startup backed by Sequoia | Preston Fore, Fortune

Earlier this month, defense tech firm Mach Industries raised $600 million in a Series C extension at a $3.7 billion valuation.

That’s more than double the $1.8 billion valuation Mach reached just three months earlier when it raised its initial $300 million Series C led by Ribbit Capital, Infinite Capital, Bedrock Capital, and Sequoia Capital. But perhaps more striking than the pace of the raises is who’s leading them: Mach, which builds autonomous defense systems, is run by a 22-year-old.

Founder and CEO Ethan Thornton launched Mach in 2023 at 19, after developing an interest in defense as a teenager. Since then, he’s built the company around a willingness to move quickly, take risks, and adapt as its technology and the broader defense industry evolve.

“You’re never going to know everything, especially when you’re starting young, and you shouldn’t expect to,” Thornton told Fortune. “If you wait until you have all the answers, you’ll probably never start.”

By 2024, Mach landed a deal with the Army Applications Laboratory to develop a vertical-takeoff precision cruise missile—and the company’s momentum has only accelerated since.

Today, the Gen Zer is running a company with six weapons programs, a 115,000-square-foot headquarters and manufacturing facility in Huntington Beach, California, and ambitions to build everything from airframes and jet engines to solid rocket motors, energetic systems, and autonomous technologies.

The company’s rapid growth comes amid a broader boom in defense tech. Allie reported earlier this year that a record $19.8 billion was deployed into the sector in the first quarter of 2026 alone. Thornton, however, is betting that Mach can do more than simply ride that wave. After several years spent developing and testing its technology, the company is now shifting its focus toward production.

“For a company like Mach, private capital lets us take risk earlier. We can build before there’s a massive program behind something, test it, learn from it and change it quickly,” Thornton told Fortune. “And because we think about manufacturing from the beginning, we’re not designing something and figuring out how to produce it years later. We’re building the product and the production capability at the same time.”

Turning teenage military interests into a defense tech unicorn

Thornton’s interest in defense started well before Mach—and before he was old enough to drive a car.

Growing up in a military family in Texas, Thornton increasingly became concerned about China’s rise and what he described as an “impending great power conflict.” By 16, he was already prototyping defense applications on his parents’ property, experimenting with hydrogen-powered weapons using materials sourced from Home Depot and Amazon.

He took that interest to MIT, where he studied aerospace (and even made the football roster) while working with the school’s federally funded defense research center, Lincoln Laboratory. Before finishing his first year, Thornton received a Thiel Fellowship and left MIT to focus full-time on his company.

Mach quickly caught the attention of Silicon Valley. In June 2023, Sequoia Capital led a $5.7 million funding round in Mach—the VC’s first investment in a hardware defense technology company. Stephanie Zhan, a Sequoia partner who led the investment, summed up Thornton’s ambitions at the time:

“Ethan is a force of nature: from his technical depth and genuine obsession with the problem to his bias for action and maturity beyond his years,” Zhan said. “Defense technology is central to our safety and security, and Mach is a step-function advancement to the state of the industry.”

For Thornton, however, the lessons from building Mach so young have been less about having all the answers than about knowing who to surround himself with.

“Find people who are better than you at the things you don’t know, who will challenge you and who believe in what you’re trying to build,” he said.

Thornton’s core advice for other young people with ambitious ideas is similarly straightforward: Don’t be afraid to fail.

“You have to be willing to learn as you go, make mistakes and keep moving. Have conviction in the problem you’re trying to solve, and then surround yourself with people who can help you solve it.”

posts.text:
ICYMI O/N

IRAN:

Trump said the Iran war was “essentially almost over” during his Nebraska speech, calling higher gasoline prices a “small price to pay” to prevent Tehran obtaining a nuclear weapon. (Iran International)  

Saudi and Yemeni forces launched an offensive to retake Mokha and ease the threat to shipping through Bab al-Mandeb, with around 100 fighters providing air cover, the Saudi-led coalition said. A Yemeni spokesman claimed control of the strait, which WSJ couldn’t independently confirm. (WSJ)    

The Houthis said they launched missile and drone attacks against Riyadh’s airport, Aramco’s Rabigh refinery and Saudi military installations in response to the offensive. Their spokesman warned airlines that Saudi airspace had become a theatre for their operations. (WSJ)  

Fars published footage claiming a fire at an Aramco facility in Jeddah following a Yemeni attack. The facility’s identity, damage and operational impact remain unconfirmed. (Fars)  

The U.S. withdrew 12 B-1 bombers from RAF Fairford over an IRGC-linked drone threat, U.S. and European officials told WSJ. Officials described a broader plot against aircraft and American pilots; British officials cautioned there was no evidence Tehran could execute an operation of that complexity. (WSJ)  

Gulf oil flows excluding Iran surged to over 81% of pre-war levels in September, data showed, led by a recovery in Saudi exports, while Iranian exports fell to zero due to a US blockade. (RTRS)

At least 50 tankers carrying Iranian oil remain backed up near Iran under the US blockade, according to United Against Nuclear Iran. Bloomberg’s preliminary tracking estimates show Iran loaded no crude onto tankers in September, the first zero-loading month since the war began. (BBG)  

Iranian Interior Minister Momeni said talks in Doha addressed Qatar and Pakistan’s mediation efforts, with proposals discussed aimed at reducing regional tensions and averting further war. (IRNA)

UN Secretary-General António Guterres arrived in Islamabad for a three-day visit, with Iran-US mediation among the subjects for talks with Pakistan’s political and military leadership. No breakthrough was announced. (IRNA)  

Recovering Hormuz crude flows aren’t resolving the diesel shortage: crude shipments reached 76% of prewar levels, but refined products accounted for just 11% of total oil flows versus over 20% before the war. Damaged refineries mean a full recovery could take well into 2027, analysts told WSJ. (WSJ)  

Trump signed an order allowing wider on-road use of tax-exempt red diesel, effectively offering a 24-cent-a-gallon federal tax saving. The IRS will waive penalties on highway sales through year-end; energy specialists warned limited distribution could constrain the benefit. (BBG)  

The World Bank warned that Asian governments’ energy subsidies may prove unsustainable, forecasting Middle East oil exports would not regain pre-war levels until mid-2027. It nevertheless raised its 2026 East Asia and Pacific growth forecast to 4.5%, citing AI investment and exports. (BBG)  

MACRO:

US borrowing costs for companies rated CCC or below reached 17%, the highest since May 2020, as the Treasury sell-off spreads into corporate credit. BofA cut its forecast for this month’s investment-grade issuance to $110bn from roughly $160bn. (FT)  

Commercial-property buyers are demanding price cuts or threatening to abandon deals as financing costs rise, WSJ reports. The share of CMBS mortgages in special servicing reached 11.42% in August, its highest since February 2013, according to Trepp. (WSJ) 

FT’s Unhedged column flags a potential dollar vulnerability: huge foreign inflows into US AI assets and falling currency hedging have left investors heavily exposed to USD. An AI reversal or renewed hedging could trigger substantial dollar selling, drawing on Nomura and BNY analysis. (FT)  

An OECD survey of 8,000 employers found just 1% of firms adopting AI were cutting headcount mainly because of the technology. FT reports economists remain sceptical of predictions of mass job losses, despite slowing entry-level tech hiring. (FT)  

HSBC maintains its call for further steepening in the U.S. 5s30s Treasury curve. Strategist Dhiraj Narula said volatility and the lack of clear technical resistance are keeping investors sidelined despite increasingly attractive long-end yields. (WSJ) 

The BoJ may signal this month that underlying inflation has roughly hit its 2% target, according to Reuters sources, highlighting its readiness to raise interest rates again in the coming months. Many in the central bank are cautious about delivering another hike this month. (RTRS)

BoJ Governor Ueda said on Tuesday it was becoming more important to anchor underlying inflation around the central bank's 2% target, signalling readiness to keep raising interest rates to blunt the risk of too-high inflation. (RTRS)

Japan’s 10-year auction was well received, where it attracted a bid-to-cover of 3.76, versus 3.29 previously and a 12-month average of 3.21; the tail narrowed to 0.02 from 0.12. JGB futures pared losses as yields above 3% brought buyers back. (BBG)  

Citi’s Tomohisa Fujiki said JGB yields are approaching their peaks, with 2.5–3% fair value for the 10-year if inflation stabilises near 2%. Citi expects curve flattening and warned crowded long-bank/short-property positioning could reverse. (BBG)  

US VP Vance told reporters that the $54bn Alaska LNG project with South Korea would proceed, despite Seoul making participation conditional on commercial viability and Trump threatening trade retaliation. South Korea said it transferred the first $2.4bn of investment funding under the US trade deal last week. (BBG)

SocGen remains neutral on Korean equities and prefers Taiwan as memory-chip earnings momentum fades and buyers disappear. Foreign investors sold $25bn of Korean stocks in August–September, while turnover has fallen around 75% from June’s peak; strategists described an “absence of marginal buyers.” (WSJ)    

South Korea’s President Lee said there were signs AI was used in attacks exposing customer data at seven financial firms. Hackers appear to have targeted third-party systems rather than core payment networks; no stolen funds have been reported. (FT)  

Australia’s Westpac consumer sentiment index fell 4.7% to 80.4 following the RBA hike and continued fuel-price pressure. Responses collected after the rate decision registered just 67.2; Westpac expects another hike in November. (BBG) 

Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers told Bloomberg TV that higher bond yields would squeeze the budget as cheap debt is refinanced. He will incorporate the impact into the year-end budget update; RBC estimates current market yields could add about A$6bn to four-year costs. (BBG)   

New Zealand’s NZIER survey showed a net 43% of firms expecting economic improvement, with seasonally adjusted confidence the strongest since 2014. Actual demand remained weak, while fewer businesses planned price rises, suggesting limited pass-through of higher costs. (BBG) 

New Zealand’s governing National Party fell to 25.9%, its weakest polling result since 2020, in an RNZ-Reid Research survey ahead of November’s election. Neither main bloc would command a majority, leaving the centrist Opportunity Party potentially holding the balance of power. (BBG)   

Germany’s coalition is struggling to agree tax measures worth more than €4bn annually, with disputes over sugar, plastics and crypto gains threatening the budget deal. One official told Bloomberg that November approval of the 2027 budget could no longer be assumed. (BBG)  

German factory orders fell 10.6% M/M in August versus -1% expected, following July’s 3.2% rise. Large orders drove the decline: excluding them, orders slipped just 0.1%, while the three-month measure remained up 1.3%. (BBG)  

Germany’s AfD is expected to secure its first regional parliament presidency in Saxony-Anhalt on Tuesday with support from the hard-left BSW. The party is separately seeking enough votes to install its first state premier. (FT)  

French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen presents plans on Tuesday to cut government spending by €25 billion ($28 billion) a year, seeking to establish her fiscal credibility in the face of a growing bond market crisis. (RTRS)

France’s 10-year borrowing costs have approached 5%, with its spread over Bunds widening by almost two-thirds in a month to around 140bp. FT reports growing investor concern that political resistance to budget cuts could turn the sell-off into a broader Eurozone crisis. (FT)  

France faces more than $1tn of debt maturities by 2030 and plans roughly $380bn of issuance next year, as traditional buyers retreat and borrowing costs approach 5%. WSJ reports debt-servicing costs are projected to rise 59% by 2030, with political paralysis undermining efforts to contain spending. (WSJ)  

French teachers are joining nationwide student protests demanding more education spending, adding pressure as the government seeks budget restraint. National Rally said it wants to avoid worsening the bond crisis and acknowledged that toppling the government could contribute to an escalation. (BBG)  

Czech inflation accelerated more than expected last month after the central bank warned that tighter monetary policy may be warranted to tame price growth. (BBG)

Philippine September CPI accelerated to 7.2% Y/Y versus 6.8% expected, ending four months of slowing inflation. Food and fuel drove the upside surprise, strengthening the case for further BSP tightening at its October 22 meeting. (BBG)

Thai September CPI rose 2.82% Y/Y versus 3.1% expected and 2.53% previously. The Commerce Ministry expects further acceleration in Q4 as fuel costs feed through, with flooding estimated to add around 0.1 percentage point to inflation. (BBG)  

EQUITIES:

OpenAI is discussing a $30bn funding round with UAE investors including MGX and with BlackRock, according to Bloomberg sources. The UAE syndicate could contribute up to $10bn; OpenAI is pitching a roughly $1.4tn pre-money valuation. (BBG)  

Wall Street banks have launched a record $60bn financing tied to Broadcom chips for Anthropic, according to the FT. (FT)  

Nvidia-backed Reflection launched its first open-weight model, Beam, targeting Chinese rivals in coding and agentic tasks. Reflection says it competes with https://t.co/da7jebtExB’s GLM-5.2 and is approaching Qwen3.8-Max; the model activates 23bn of its 501bn parameters per task. (RTRS)  

SemiAnalysis estimates Claude subscriptions offer roughly five times the API-equivalent value of comparable mid-tier ChatGPT plans following OpenAI’s limit reductions. Its analysis highlights subscription subsidies as a significant drag on AI-lab inference margins. (SemiAnalysis)  

Google is nearing a multiyear nuclear-power agreement worth at least $1bn with Constellation, according to Bloomberg sources. An announcement could come this week; the capacity and location have not been established. (BBG) 

AMD’s Lisa Su said demand still exceeds supply across CPUs, GPUs and AI products, and AMD will increase its previously announced $10bn Taiwan supply-chain investment. Supply should rise substantially in 2027, but customers could absorb more; planning now extends three to five years ahead. (China Times) 

OpenAI and Anthropic told Australian parliament on Tuesday they would welcome laws requiring them to report data breaches carried out by their AI agents, acknowledging the decision to notify authorities was currently at their discretion. (RTRS)

Oracle’s 2025 healthcare breach affected nearly 20 million people, according to newly reported disclosures from the Texas attorney general. The compromised information included Social Security numbers and medical records; the scale had not previously been disclosed. (BBG)   

Banks are expanding into Asian GPU lending, broadening funding for the AI buildout despite uncertainty over chip depreciation. Citi, JPMorgan, Barclays, Deutsche Bank, Santander and SMBC are evaluating GPU-linked loans, according to Bloomberg sources. (BBG)  

KKR’s retail private-credit fund K-FITS will exceed its 5% quarterly redemption cap to meet all requests, after withdrawals reached 5.06% of shares versus 3.43% previously. The fund cited sufficient liquidity to fulfil the requests in full. (BBG)  

DayOne Data Centers publicly filed for a US IPO after previously exploring a raise of up to $5bn at around $20bn valuation. Its filing showed first-half revenue rising to $512m from $151.5m, while its net loss widened to $81.9m. (BBG)  

NextEra’s $67bn Dominion takeover faces growing political opposition in Virginia, with Governor Abigail Spanberger seeking concessions on electricity bills, jobs and investment. FT reports the backlash is raising pressure for tougher approval conditions despite improved customer credits and employment guarantees. (FT)  

Korean memory suppliers are quoting sharply higher HBM4 long-term contract prices for 2027, according to DIGITIMES supply-chain reporting: approximately $1,400–1,600 versus $500–550 in 2026. (DIGITIMES)  

Seagate and Toshiba are competing for TDK’s hard-drive magnetic-heads business in a potential multibillion-dollar deal, Bloomberg sources said. TDK is the only independent supplier of the component; its shares jumped 7.3% as the bidders seek to secure AI storage supply. (BBG)  

DeepSeek is close to raising at least 80bn yuan ($12bn), exceeding its original 50bn-yuan target, according to Bloomberg sources. Tencent and CATL are among the largest backers, with signed term sheets potentially taking the round toward 100bn yuan ahead of an early-2027 IPO. (BBG)  

Moonshot AI completed its final private funding round at roughly $50bn valuation and is targeting a Hong Kong IPO in Q1 2027, according to Bloomberg sources. Early investor meetings could begin this month; the company has considered raising up to $5bn. (BBG)  

Grab and GoTo face mounting pressure from driver protests, high fuel costs and tighter commission rules across south-east Asia. Their long-running merger talks remain on hold because of Indonesian policy uncertainty, according to FT sources. (FT)  

CVC increased its Recordati offer to €53 per share from €51.29, valuing the pharmaceutical company at €10.5bn. The revised bid remains below the €60 sought by shareholder Palliser; Recordati closed Monday at €52.20. (BBG)  

BPCE acquired roughly 7% of Banco Sabadell, will receive board representation and committed to keeping its stake below 10%. The banks described the investment as friendly and will explore cooperation across investment banking, leasing and consumer credit. (BBG)

In a matter of weeks, President Trump has locked in a run of steel, nuclear, gas, shipbuilding, and medical manufacturing commitments that will hire American workers and strengthen American security.
• President Trump announced that Mesabi Metallics will build a $15 billion steel complex in Iowa the largest steel plant ever built in the United States. Fed by American iron ore and driven by the Trump Administration’s steel tariffs, the fully integrated mine-to-mill complex will create 1,750 new, permanent jobs, support up to 6,000 construction jobs, and generate an estimated $95 billion in economic output.

• President Trump and Anduril announced Arsenal-2, the biggest new American shipyard push since World War II, now moving forward in Maryland. The yard will produce critical Virginia-class components and large assemblies, create about 3,100 direct jobs, and support more than 11,000 indirect jobs. Anduril is investing $3.7 billion in private capital; the Navy is putting up to $2.9 billion behind it as part of the Trump Administration’s push to reshore America’s defense industrial base.

• President Trump unveiled a South Korean energy investment package of up to $200 billion in the United States. The package includes as much as $120 billion to build eight large-scale nuclear plants, $54 billion tied to the Alaska LNG pipeline, and $22.3 billion for a six-gigawatt natural gas power facility in Texas.

• Vice President Vance announced that the Department of Energy will invest $150 million to advance a major new transmission line in Alaska. The project includes 223 miles linking the Beluga power station on the southern coast with Healy in the Interior, a corridor serving ports and nearly three-quarters of the state’s population.

• Becton Dickinson announced a $19 billion U.S. investment under a landmark partnership with the Trump Administration, including $3 billion to expand American manufacturing. BD will produce 100% of the needles it sells in America with American-made steel and expand domestic output of essential products.

• AstraZeneca announced a $1 billion investment in Massachusetts under the $50 billion investment commitment it made in its Most Favored Nation agreement with the Trump Administration. The company is expanding its domestic research and manufacturing operation and growing its domestic workforce.

October 8th, 2026.

Nuclear Communications

Hard Tech Headlines:

- @HadrianInc has secured a seven-year deal with @LockheedMartin to integrate its advanced manufacturing technology into Lockheed Martin's Missiles and Fire Control operations, bringing in its Opus software platform for factory automation, manufacturing capabilities, and its national manufacturing network.

- @MilremR has secured a partnership with Chugach Alaska Corporation focused on the potential for Chugach to manufacture Milrem’s unmanned ground vehicles in the United States. Chugach is one of Alaska’s largest defense contractors.

- XTEND AI Robotics has secured a $40.5M order from the Department of War focused on delivering 6,000 drones.

- Prysmian has acquired Xtera Topco Limited, a developer of submarine telecommunications technology, in a deal valued at $65 million.

- The U.S. Air Force has awarded Raytheon a contract worth up to $8 billion to modernize critical communications systems designed to keep America's nuclear forces connected during a potential nuclear war.

- @deployrobo has launched out of YC. The startup is deploying robotic arms for commercial operations, with a business model where customers pay for completed robotic work rather than the robots themselves.

- The U.S. Army has selected five winners of its competition focused on forward-deployable power generation and energy storage. The winners include United Protective Technologies, Our Next Energy, @chariotdefense, PacMar Technologies, and Harbinger Praesidia.

- @SkydioHQ has launched ISR Command, enabling a single operator to control two X10D drones for persistent battlefield surveillance, autonomous target tracking, and strike coordination, laying the groundwork for larger-scale drone fleet orchestration.

- Molagri has secured $5.8M in pre-seed and seed funding. The Toronto-based startup develops biopesticides designed to overcome insect resistance to conventional pesticides.

- Giraffe Bio has secured a $6.4M seed round led by Orion Industrial Ventures. The Argentina-based company uses synthetic biology to improve copper extraction.

- The U.S. Space Force has launched Space Forces Special Operations, based in Florida.

- @AeonIndustrial has announced plans for a new 140,000-square-foot manufacturing facility in Texas to scale American production of motors, fuzes, seekers, and complete weapons systems.

- The Ohio Department of Transportation has deployed two drone docking stations in Cincinnati for critical infrastructure inspections and construction monitoring.

- Consor has acquired ConeLabs, which develops digital twins for critical infrastructure.

- SAFE has secured a $10M U.S. Marine Corps contract focused on unmanned ground vehicles for expeditionary logistics, with the ability to load pallets weighing up to 10,000 pounds.
